section.title: Warning Against Falling Away
section.sectionRationale: Before developing the Melchizedek priesthood, the writer pauses to rebuke his readers' spiritual dullness and to sound the sharpest of his warnings. He urges them to press on to maturity, warns of the impossibility of renewal for those who fall away after tasting the heavenly gift, and then expresses confidence that they will show the diligence that accompanies salvation.
section.thesis: The readers have become dull and immature when they ought to be teachers; so the writer calls them to press on from the foundations to maturity, warns with terrible seriousness that those who taste the blessings of the gospel and then fall away cannot be renewed to repentance, and yet expresses confident hope that they will persevere in the diligence and love that accompany salvation.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the rebuke of dullness and the call to grow up from milk to solid food; the solemn warning against falling away, illustrated by fruitful and worthless land; and the writer's confidence in the readers, grounded in God's justice and their proven love.

verses.text: We have much to say about this, but it is hard to explain, because you are {{nothros|dull}} of hearing.
Although by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to reteach you the basic principles of God’s word. You need milk, not solid food!
For everyone who lives on milk is still an infant, inexperienced in the message of righteousness.
But solid food is for the mature, who by constant use have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil.

units.label: Go on to maturity
units.note: leave the elementary and press on

verses.text: Therefore let us leave the elementary teachings about Christ and go on to {{teleiotes|maturity}}, not laying again the foundation of {{metanoia|repentance}} from dead works, and of faith in God,
instruction about baptisms, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment.
And this we will do, if God permits.
It is {{adynatos|impossible}} for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have shared in the Holy Spirit,
who have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the coming age,
and then have fallen away, to be restored to repentance, because they themselves are crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame.
For land that drinks in the rain often falling on it and that produces a crop useful to those for whom it is tended receives the blessing of God.
But land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless, and its curse is imminent. In the end it will be burned.
Even though we speak like this, beloved, we are convinced of better things in your case, things that accompany salvation.
For God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name as you have ministered to the saints and continue to do so.
We want each of you to show this same diligence to the very end, in order to make your hope sure.
Then you will not be {{nothros|sluggish}}, but will imitate those who through faith and patience inherit what has been promised.

nothros.gloss: Sluggish, dull, slow. The readers had become dull of hearing, no longer growing; the writer uses the same word again in 6:12, urging them not to remain sluggish but to press on with the diligence of persevering faith.

teleiotes.gloss: Maturity, completeness, full growth. The goal is to move beyond the elementary foundations to mature understanding and steady discernment, the solid food fit for those trained by constant use.

metanoia.gloss: Repentance, a change of mind and turning from sin. It belongs to the foundation of the Christian life; the warning is that those who taste the gospel's blessings and then fall away cannot be brought back again to this repentance.

adynatos.gloss: Impossible, without power to do a thing. The stark word that opens the warning: for those who fall away after such privileges, renewal to repentance is impossible, since to reject Christ knowingly is to trample the only remedy there is.

basic.context: The writer wants to teach the readers deep truth about Christ's priesthood, but they have become spiritually lazy, still needing milk when they should be teachers. So he calls them to grow up, then delivers his most severe warning: those who have shared richly in the blessings of the gospel and then deliberately turn away cannot be brought back to repentance. Yet he ends warmly, confident they will show the fruit that belongs to salvation.
basic.hermeneutics: Hold the warning and the reassurance together; both are in the same passage. The warning is real and searching; the confidence in verses 9 to 12 shows its pastoral purpose is to produce perseverance, not despair. Read the fruitful and barren land as the two possible outcomes of the same gospel privileges.
basic.originalLanguages: The readers are nōthros, dull and sluggish; the call is to teleiotēs, maturity. The foundation includes metanoia, repentance. And the warning opens with adynatos, impossible: renewal cannot happen for the deliberate apostate.
basic.typology: The image of land receiving rain recalls Isaiah's vineyard and the covenant blessings and curses: the same gospel that blesses the fruitful becomes judgment on the barren. The thorns and thistles echo the curse of Genesis 3.
basic.christ: To fall away is to crucify the Son of God again and hold Him up to open shame, treating the one and only remedy as worthless. The passage magnifies Christ by showing that to reject Him is to reject the only salvation there is.
basic.god: God is just; He will not forget the readers' love and service. God is also the one who permits growth, if He wills, and whose judgment falls on fruitless ground. His justice grounds both the warning and the assurance.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 10 gives a parallel warning. Isaiah 5 pictures the vineyard that yields wild grapes. 2 Peter 2 describes those who knew the way and turned back.
basic.oneStory: God's gospel word, like rain, falls on all who hear; the story asks what fruit it will bear. Those who receive it in faith press on to inherit the promise; those who spurn it face the curse.

context.literary:
This long section is a digression with a plan. After naming Melchizedek in 5:10 the writer says 'we have much to say about this,' and then stops to deal with the hearers themselves. The section moves in four steps. A rebuke, 5:11 to 14, is followed by a summons, 6:1 to 3, then the warning proper, 6:4 to 8, and finally the reassurance, 6:9 to 12. It is a pastoral sandwich, with sharp words in the middle and warm ones at both ends.

The rebuke is organised by one image, food. Milk belongs to infants and solid food to the mature, and the difference is not a matter of intelligence but of use. The mature have 'trained their senses' by 'constant use,' so maturity is practised discernment, not information.

The warning is itself built like a ladder. Four clauses, enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit, tasted the goodness of the word and the powers of the age to come, pile up the privileges before the one sudden hinge, 'and then have fallen away.' Then comes the farming parable of verses 7 and 8, which gives the same truth in picture form: the same rain, two different harvests.

The reassurance reverses the tone. 'Beloved,' a word found nowhere else in the letter, signals the shift, and the phrase 'better things' picks up the letter's favourite comparative. The section then closes by tying back to its start: the readers who were 'dull,' 5:11, must not be 'sluggish,' 6:12. The same Greek word is used in both places, framing the whole passage with a single call to wake up.
context.historical:
The readers had been believers 'by this time' long enough to be teachers, so the church was probably a second generation, converted through those who heard the Lord, 2:3. Hebrews 10:32 to 34 remembers the early days of insult and loss of property, and the question was whether they would stay. Many had a way out: Judaism was a recognised religion in the Roman world, and a return to it might have seemed to offer safety.

The warning has to be heard in that setting. To 'fall away' is not to commit an ordinary sin, such as stumbling in temper, but to abandon Christ publicly and go back to the old life. The writer says elsewhere that such a person has 'trampled on the Son of God,' 10:29. The seriousness comes from how much the readers had received and how final a repudiation would be.

The list of basics in 6:1 and 2 is familiar from Jewish and early Christian instruction: repentance and faith, washings, the laying on of hands, resurrection and judgment. The first readers could have found most of these in a synagogue too, and that is part of the danger. If they never went beyond them, Christianity would look like an addition to Judaism and not its fulfilment.

The agricultural picture would have been immediate to people who lived by the seasons. Palestine depends on the early and later rains, and Deuteronomy 11:10 to 17 tells Israel that rain was God's gift and withheld rain His discipline. A field that drank the rain and still bore only thorns was a field that had failed its keeper, and the writer uses a scene any farmer would grasp.
context.canonical:
The passage belongs with the letter's five warnings, 2:1 to 4, 3:7 to 4:13, 5:11 to 6:12, 10:19 to 39 and 12:14 to 29. Each says in a different way that the greater the revelation, the greater the danger of neglecting it. The two closest siblings are 10:26 to 31, which speaks of 'deliberately' going on sinning and of trampling the Son of God, and 12:16 and 17, where Esau finds 'no ground for repentance' though he sought the blessing with tears.

The Old Testament background is the covenant. Numbers 15:30 and 31 separates sin done unknowingly from sin done defiantly, and says the second blasphemes the LORD. Deuteronomy 28 and 29 pair blessings with curses. Isaiah 5:1 to 7 sings of a vineyard that bore sour fruit and was left a wasteland, with thorns and briers growing up, and the clouds commanded not to rain on it. Hebrews 6:7 and 8 makes a similar point from the same ground.

Other New Testament writers hold the same tension. Jesus warns that branches that do not remain in Him are thrown away, John 15:6, and that some who receive the word with joy have no root and fall away in testing, Luke 8:13. Peter says that those who turn back after knowing the way of righteousness are worse off than before, 2 Peter 2:20 to 22. John writes that some who left 'did not belong to us,' 1 John 2:19. And alongside all of these stand the great assurances, John 10:28 and 29 and Romans 8:38 and 39, which Hebrews' own 6:9 to 12 and 6:18 to 20 echo.

The thorns and thistles of verse 8 reach back to the curse of Genesis 3:17 and 18, so the passage ties apostasy to the curse on the ground.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants to produce two things at once: alarm and hope. He is not trying to settle an academic question about the limits of salvation. He is trying to wake people who have grown slack. The sequence of the section shows that. He first shames them for their dullness, then calls them forward, then paints the worst case so that they will see where drifting ends, and then, quickly, tells them he does not think they are there.

The rebuke has a practical edge. Spiritual maturity is shown by the ability to tell good from evil, which comes from using the word, not from merely hearing it. He wants the readers to become people who can teach, and so he sets before them an agenda: go on.

The warning is meant to be taken at face value. The writer believes the danger is real for those he addresses, and does not soften it by saying that it could never happen to a Christian. At the same time, he insists he is 'convinced of better things.' These are not contradictory in his mind. A warning is one of the means God uses to keep His people, and a person who hears it and presses on is showing the fruit of salvation.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes a spiritual condition in 5:11 to 14, a possibility in 6:4 to 8, and a confidence in 6:9 to 12. It prescribes in 6:1 to 3 and 6:11 and 12: go on to maturity, show diligence to the end, imitate those who inherit the promise through faith and patience.

It is important not to turn the description of the impossibility into a general rule about every failure. The text does not say that a believer who sins grievously, or who is cold for a season, cannot be restored. Peter denied Jesus three times and was restored, John 21:15 to 19, and Hebrews 12:12 elsewhere tells believers to strengthen weak knees. The passage speaks about a settled, public abandonment of Christ by those who have known Him.

It is also not a licence for despair. A reader who fears that he has committed the sin in view can note that the very concern about it is the opposite of the hardened state the text describes. The right use of the passage is to move toward Christ with fresh seriousness. In pastoral practice the passage serves as a safeguard against the idea that a past decision makes present perseverance unnecessary.

debates.question: Who are those described in 6:4-6, and can genuine believers lose salvation?

views.label: Professing members who were never truly regenerate
views.case: The rich descriptions, enlightened, tasted, shared, portray real exposure to the covenant community's blessings without saving union with Christ. The verbs say 'tasted,' not 'ate,' and Jesus describes seed on rocky ground that springs up without root, Luke 8:13. When such people fall away they show they never truly belonged, 1 John 2:19, and the fruit of verses 7 to 9 distinguishes true believers whose lives yield a crop.

views.label: A real warning that functions to preserve God's people
views.case: The language is that of genuine gospel privilege, and the warning is addressed to the church as a real danger. God uses such warnings as the means by which His people persevere, so those who truly heed it are kept. Hebrews 3:14 makes sharing in Christ depend on holding firm to the end, which fits a warning that has real force.

views.label: A real possibility: believers can fall away
views.case: Others take the words at face value as describing true Christians who can finally and fatally leave Christ. They read 'shared in the Holy Spirit' as a mark of real conversion and point to Hebrews 10:26 to 29, where the sinner was 'sanctified' by the blood of the covenant. This reading has been held by many in the Wesleyan tradition and by much of the early church.

views.label: A hypothetical case underscoring the gravity of apostasy
views.case: Some read the passage as pressing the logic of what deliberate, final rejection of Christ would mean, namely no remaining sacrifice, so as to drive the readers to press on rather than to describe those already lost.

debates.bearing: All the historic orthodox readings agree on the practical point: to knowingly and finally reject Christ after tasting the gospel is beyond remedy, so the reader must take the warning to heart and persevere. And verses 9 to 12 assure that persevering love and diligence are the marks of those who are truly saved.

debates.question: What does 'impossible to restore' mean, and what do the present participles of verse 6 tell us?

views.label: Impossible for as long as they crucify Him
views.case: The participles 'crucifying' and 'subjecting Him to open shame' are in the present tense, and some read them as saying that restoration is impossible while the rejection continues. That would leave open a change of heart. The difficulty is that the verse says 'impossible,' and the same word is used of the impossibility of God lying, 6:18.

views.label: Impossible because the act is final
views.case: Others take the participles as giving the reason: the person who turns away from the one sacrifice has nothing else to turn to, since 'no further sacrifice for sins remains,' 10:26. The impossibility is not that God cannot forgive but that there is no second Christ and no second cross.

views.label: Impossible for us to bring about
views.case: A third view holds that the verse speaks of what human teachers can do. Believers cannot restore those who have openly repudiated Christ, but Jesus said that with God all things are possible, Mark 10:27, and so the door remains open from His side.

debates.bearing: The three views agree that the case is grave and that there is no second way of salvation apart from Christ. Where they differ is on whether the text comments on God's freedom, and most readers will prefer to leave that to God and to press the practical call.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for the readers' condition in 5:11 and 6:12 is the same in the Greek, nothros, translated 'dull' in the first place and 'sluggish' in the second. It occurs in the New Testament only in these two verses, and the repetition frames the whole passage. They were slow in hearing, and they must not become slow in living. The phrase 'dull of hearing' is more literally 'sluggish in the ears,' which suggests that they are not deaf but lazy listeners.

In 5:14 the 'senses' that are to be trained are a noun found only here in the New Testament, and 'trained' is the verb from which we get 'gymnasium.' It is the word for athletic exercise. 'By constant use' translates a word for a settled habit. The picture is a trained athlete whose reflexes are formed by repeated practice, and the training is to 'distinguish good from evil,' that is, moral discernment.

Verse 6:1 says 'let us go on' in a passive form, literally 'let us be carried along,' which suggests that the movement is something that happens to those who yield to it, as a boat is carried by the wind. In 6:2 the 'baptisms' are a plural, and the word used is the one for ritual washings, not the usual word for Christian baptism. This is why the BSB footnote suggests 'cleansing rites.' The teaching had to include the difference between Christian baptism and the Jewish washings.

The central phrase of 6:4 is 'once enlightened.' 'Once' here is the word the letter normally uses of what is done once for all, as in 9:26 and 9:28. The verb 'enlightened' returns in 10:32, where the readers are told to remember the days after they were enlightened. 'Tasted' is the same verb used of Jesus tasting death for everyone in 2:9, which shows that it can mean a full experience and not only a sip. 'Shared' translates the word for partners, used of believers in the heavenly calling, 3:1, and in Christ, 3:14.

'Fallen away' in 6:6 is a verb that occurs only here in the New Testament, a compound meaning to fall to one side, as from a path. It is not the common word for 'stumble.' The word 'impossible' is also used in 6:18 of God lying, and in 10:4 of the blood of bulls and goats taking away sins. The writer reserves the term for what cannot be.

In 6:8 the pairing 'thorns and thistles' is the pairing of the Septuagint of Genesis 3:18. The word 'worthless' is the same one Paul uses of being 'disqualified' in 1 Corinthians 9:27, a word for what fails a test. And in 6:10 the word for 'unjust,' adikos, is the negation of 'righteous,' so the sentence reads that God would be unrighteous if He forgot their love.

typology.type: The vineyard that bore sour fruit, Isaiah 5:1-7
typology.fulfillment: God planted, fenced and tended a vineyard and looked for good grapes, but found sour ones. He then removed the hedge and commanded the clouds not to rain on it. Hebrews 6:7 and 8 borrows the vocabulary: land watered with rain, thorns, and the end of burning. The correspondence is that privilege creates responsibility. In Jesus the picture is turned toward Him as the true vine, John 15:1 to 6, and toward the branches that do not remain, which are thrown into the fire. The type falls short in that Isaiah's vineyard is a nation, while Hebrews speaks of individuals within a community.

typology.type: The ground cursed with thorns, Genesis 3:17-18
typology.fulfillment: The curse on the ground produced thorns and thistles as the sign of the fall. Hebrews 6:8 uses the same pair to name worthless land, suggesting that those who abandon the gospel return to the condition of the first rebels. The correspondence is that rain from God yields fruit only where the soil responds. Jesus took the curse upon Himself, Galatians 3:13, and wore a crown of thorns, Matthew 27:29. The type falls short because the land in Hebrews has a choice in a way the ground of Eden did not, so the image is of responsibility, not only of fate.

A generation that saw God's works, heard His voice and ate manna still refused to enter the land, and none of them did. Hebrews 3:7 to 4:13 has already made the point, and 6:4 and 5 says the same of the church: those who have tasted the heavenly gift may still fall. The escalation is that the privileges of the new covenant are greater, with the Spirit and the powers of the age to come. The type falls short because Israel's failure was followed by a new generation entering, while the final rejection of Christ has no second sacrifice.

typology.type: Esau who sold his birthright, Genesis 25:29-34
typology.fulfillment: Esau traded a lasting privilege for a single meal, and Hebrews 12:16 and 17 says that afterward he found no ground for repentance though he sought the blessing with tears. The correspondence with Hebrews 6 is that a person can despise what God has given and find that the moment has passed. In Christ the blessing is greater than a birthright, and the warning is correspondingly greater. The type falls short because Esau lost an earthly inheritance, whereas apostasy forfeits what Christ alone can give.

study.christ:
This passage looks at Christ from the underside of the warning. The most startling phrase is in verse 6, that those who fall away are 'crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame.' The sentence reveals how high the writer's Christology is. To walk away from Jesus is not to leave a teacher but to side with the crowd at Golgotha, to say that He deserved the cross.

It also shows why there is no second route. The whole letter is built on the claim that Christ's sacrifice was made once, 9:26 to 28, 10:10. The impossibility of renewal is the other face of that sufficiency. If one offering has been made and refused, there is no other to take its place. The point is not a lack of power in Christ but an abundance that cannot be repeated, since His death is complete.

Christ is also the source of the blessings that verses 4 and 5 list. Enlightenment, the heavenly gift, the Spirit, the goodness of the word, the powers of the age to come, all of these come through Him. The one who gave them is the one who is rejected. It makes the apostate's act the more tragic: he spurns the giver along with the gifts.

The 'maturity' to which verse 1 calls the readers is bound to Christ's own completeness. The word echoes 5:9, where He was 'made perfect.' The one who was perfected through suffering leads those who follow Him into maturity, 2:10. Christ is the pattern and the means of growth, and the 'solid food' of 5:14 is the teaching about His priesthood to which the letter turns next.

The hope in verses 9 to 12 is also Christ-centred, though He is not named. 'Things that accompany salvation' are what He gives, and the promise to Abraham that follows in 6:13 to 20 will culminate in Jesus the forerunner.

Care should be taken not to over-read. The passage does not teach that the sin of verse 6 is committed by any lapse, nor does it say how God deals with those whom He restores after a failure. The way Christ appears in this text is as the one whose single sacrifice is the only hope, and whose rejection is therefore the only unforgivable error. Hearers who feel the weight of the warning are not driven away from Him but pressed toward Him, since He alone can keep them from stumbling, Jude 24.
study.god:
The God of this passage is both searching and just. Verse 10 says plainly, 'God is not unjust.' The whole section turns on that sentence. It is the ground of the warning, because a just God takes seriously the rejection of His Son, and it is the ground of the reassurance, because a just God does not forget love shown to His name. His justice works in both directions.

He is the God who remembers. 'He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name.' Throughout the Old Testament memory is an active thing in God. He remembered Noah, Genesis 8:1, and He remembered His covenant, Exodus 2:24. Here He remembers ministry to the saints, and that is a remarkable word for those who were growing tired: no act of service is lost.

He is the God who speaks a word that exposes. The writer has just said that the word of God discerns the heart, 4:12, and this passage makes the same point in a rebuke. What the readers 'ought' to be and what they are is now open. God is not content that people live on milk forever.

He is the God who gives rain freely. Verse 7 says the land 'drinks in the rain often falling on it.' The rain is grace, repeated and unearned. The difference lies in the soil, not in the sky. God's goodness is steady, and what He asks is a response. That corrects any idea that God is sparing with His gifts.

He is the God who disciplines in love. The thorn-and-fire language is serious, but the passage does not leave readers there. In 12:5 to 11 the same letter shows God training His sons through hardship. A warning that moves people to repent is itself an act of care.

He holds together severity and kindness. Romans 11:22 puts it in a short line, 'Consider the kindness and severity of God.' Hebrews 6 shows both side by side, within a few verses.

For worship, the passage asks for sobriety and gladness together. We are not to be careless about the privileges we have received, and we are not to live in fear that God is waiting to catch us out. The right posture is that of the farmer's field, open to the rain and ready to bear fruit, and trusting the God who will not forget what has been done for His name.

crossReferences.note: The second great warning repeats the pattern of 6:4 to 6: deliberate sin after the knowledge of the truth leaves no further sacrifice. It adds the picture of trampling the Son of God and insulting the Spirit of grace, and it too is followed by a call to remember earlier endurance.

Esau sold his birthright for a single meal and later found no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears. It is the Old Testament case the writer uses to show that some opportunities, once despised, are not returned.
The vineyard planted with care yields sour grapes, and God withdraws the hedge and the rain. The thorns and briers, and the withheld rain, supply the images of Hebrews 6:7 and 8.
The ground is cursed and brings forth thorns and thistles. Hebrews 6:8 reuses the pair to describe worthless land whose end is burning, so apostasy is set against the curse of the fall.

A person who sins defiantly blasphemes the LORD and is cut off, in contrast with the unintentional sinner for whom sacrifice is provided. It is the background for the distinction between weakness, 5:2, and deliberate rejection.

Seed on rocky ground is received with joy but has no root, and in testing it falls away. Jesus names the same pattern of a joyful beginning that fails under pressure which Hebrews 6 fears for its readers.
Jesus says branches that do not remain in Him are gathered, thrown into the fire and burned. It matches the end of the land in Hebrews 6:8 and shows that fruit-bearing is the sign of remaining.

Those who escape the world's corruption through knowing Christ and are then entangled again end worse than they began. Peter's proverbs about the dog and the pig are the New Testament's own commentary on the danger in Hebrews 6.

Paul gave the Corinthians milk, not solid food, because they were still infants in Christ. It shows that the milk and solid food language of Hebrews 5:12 and 13 was a shared pastoral image, applied to believers who had not grown.

Some went out from us, but they did not belong to us, for if they had they would have remained. John gives one way of reading those who fall away in Hebrews 6, and it fits with the call to endurance in Hebrews 3:14.

The first warning urges the brothers to take care that no one has an unbelieving heart that turns from the living God, and says we share in Christ if we hold firmly to the end. The pattern of 6:4 to 12 grows from this.

He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus. It stands beside the warnings of Hebrews as the promise on which the writer's confidence of 'better things' rests.

study.oneStory:
The Bible keeps asking what a people will do with what they are given. Adam and Eve had the garden and one word of warning, and they ate. Israel had the exodus, the cloud, the manna and the law, and in the wilderness they hardened their hearts, Hebrews 3:8. The prophets told of vineyards that gave sour fruit. Hebrews 5:11 to 6:12 asks the same question of those who had received something even greater, the Son, the Spirit and the powers of the coming age.

That is why the passage speaks of land and of rain. The rain is the gospel, repeated and free, and the land is the people. The harvest is the life that results. This is the shape of the whole Bible: God gives, and the giving calls for fruit. When it is not forthcoming, the curse that came in Genesis 3, thorns and thistles, returns.

The passage also shows how God holds the story together. He warns because He wants His people to arrive. The warnings of Hebrews are the same kind as those in Deuteronomy, sharp because the stakes are real. And alongside them God has made promises, to Abraham in the verses that immediately follow, 6:13 to 20, that are sure because He swore them by Himself. The rest of the letter will say the same of a new covenant sealed by blood.

For the believer today the passage sits between creation's gift and the new creation's inheritance. 'Those who through faith and patience inherit what has been promised,' 6:12, are the ones whom the story is moving toward. The writer asks his readers to imitate them, which means to see themselves as part of the long line of Abel, Enoch, Noah and Abraham that chapter 11 will name.

The ending is in the new creation, where the curse of Genesis 3 is gone, Revelation 22:3. There, those who held fast, bearing the fruit that goes with salvation, enter the rest that Hebrews 4:9 promised. The land that drank the rain is then a garden, and those who endured see His face.

quiz.q: Why does the writer rebuke his readers at the start of this passage?

options.text: They have become dull and immature, needing milk when they should be teachers.
options.note: Verses 11 to 14 rebuke their spiritual sluggishness.

options.text: They knew too much and were arrogant.
options.note: The problem is immaturity and dullness, not excessive knowledge.

options.text: They had never heard the gospel.
options.note: They had heard much and should be teachers by now.

options.text: They were too advanced for his teaching.
options.note: The opposite: they had regressed to needing milk.

quiz.q: What is the seriousness of the warning in 6:4-6?

options.text: Those who fall away after tasting the gospel cannot be renewed to repentance.

options.note: The warning concerns deliberate falling away, not ordinary failures.

options.text: There are no real consequences to turning from Christ.
options.note: The warning is precisely about grave consequences.

options.text: Only outward church membership is at stake.
options.note: Far more than membership is at stake; it is renewal to repentance itself.

quiz.q: What does falling away do to Christ, according to verse 6?

options.text: It crucifies the Son of God again and subjects Him to open shame.
options.note: Apostasy treats the crucified Lord as worthless.

options.text: It has no bearing on Christ at all.
options.note: It directly dishonours the Son of God.
The offence named is against Christ Himself.

options.text: It insults the Spirit of grace, though it leaves Christ untouched.
options.note: Insulting the Spirit of grace is named in verse 29, but the point of verse 6 is that apostasy re-crucifies the Son and shames Him, so He is not left untouched.

quiz.q: How does the writer balance the warning with hope in verses 9 to 12?

options.text: He is confident of better things for them, since God justly remembers their love and service.
options.note: Verses 9 to 10 express confidence grounded in God's justice and their fruit.

options.text: He withdraws the warning as a mistake.
options.note: The warning stands; he adds confident hope alongside it.

options.text: He says their past service earns them salvation.
options.note: Their love evidences salvation; it does not earn it.

options.text: He tells them nothing more is required of them.
options.note: He urges continued diligence to the very end.

questions: The readers had stalled and needed milk again. Are there areas where your faith has stopped growing, and what would pressing on to maturity look like?
The warning is severe, yet meant to produce perseverance, not despair. How do you hold godly seriousness and settled assurance together?
To turn from Christ is to treat His cross as worthless. How does this deepen your sense of what Christ's sacrifice is worth?
God is not unjust and remembers your love shown to His name. How does that steady you when your service feels unnoticed?
We are called to imitate those who through faith and patience inherit the promise. Whose persevering faith could you learn from and follow?

translationNotes.note: 'Repentance from dead works' can also be rendered repentance from acts that lead to death; it names the turning that begins the Christian life.
Verses 5 and 6 run on as one thought, describing people who tasted the gospel's powers and then fell away.

'Crucifying the Son of God all over again' translates a participle that may be read 'while they crucify', stressing that apostasy repeats the rejection of the cross and holds Christ up to public shame.
